sections.text: A Composer Building Apps

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: I'll get straight to the point. Why is a composer building apps?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I get asked that a lot, but I never have a good answer ready, you know?

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Then let me walk through it step by step. First, what are you building?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I'm building a few tools for music production under a brand called MUED. There's MUEDnote for production logs, MUEDear for ear training, MUEDlobe for cognitive profiling, and MUEDial for online mixing.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: They all start with MUED.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Yeah, each one gets its own name based on what it does. The main one is MUEDnote—it records the decisions you make during production. Why you chose that tempo, why you went with that chord. That kind of thing.
It Started as Something Completely Different

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Was MUEDnote always a logging app?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Not even close. Originally I was trying to build an LMS—a Learning Management System—for music lessons.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Why music lessons?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I figured lessons were the one thing in music that actually worked as a business, right? When I was thinking about what to do next with my production company, that seemed like a natural starting point. And I was teaching programming on the side at the time—that's where I first came across the whole LMS concept.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You learned about LMS not from the music world, but from your experience as a programming instructor.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Exactly. I thought, "Oh, so there's a system that lets anyone deliver consistent-quality lessons." I figured we could bring that into our music teaching and systematize the whole thing.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: But then the direction changed.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Honestly? I don't think music lessons themselves have that much value.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: ...That's a pretty bold statement from someone who was about to build an education platform.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I'm not saying lessons are useless. But I went pro as a self-taught musician. No school, no mentor. What I actually needed wasn't lessons—it was a system that supports you while you teach yourself.
I Kept Cutting Until This Was All That Was Left

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: How did it evolve from an LMS?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I just kept stripping features away. Auth, servers, payments—all the stuff I'd piled on over two or three years, I ended up removing all of it.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Why?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Because none of it needed to be built from scratch. Transcription? Whisper. Payments? Stripe. Scheduling? The OS handles it. Just use what already exists. The only thing worth building yourself is the stuff nobody else can replace.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: So what was left?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Ear training and a blog.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: ...That's it?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That's it. But those two things can't be replaced by AI. Ear training is a physical skill—you can't ask AI to "train my ears" and actually get better. And the blog—the production log—is a record of your own decisions. The act of writing it is the whole point.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You spent two to three years stripping away a grand vision, and what remained was only what couldn't be replaced.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Don't make it sound cool. I was just wandering in the dark for two or three years.
Where MUEDnote Stands Now

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: So where is MUEDnote at right now?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Honestly, a lot of it has been a failure.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What kind of failure?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: It was the first app I built, so I poured way too much into the philosophy—"why production logs matter," "why you need to put things into words.” The implementation didn't keep up. I can talk about the vision all day, but when someone asks "okay, but how does it actually feel to use?"—that's where it falls short.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: That stings.
Every time I build something new, I see what I should've done the last time.
sections.speaker: kimny
kimny
sections.text: Yeah, it does. But because MUEDnote failed, I was able to go all-in on simplicity with MUEDear—just "listen to A and B, pick the right one." And MUEDial I could boil down to "mix through chat.” Every time I build something new, I see what I should've done the last time.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Is that why there are four products?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Totally. If I'd only worked on MUEDnote, I'd still be polishing the philosophy while the implementation lagged behind. Building other apps is what finally taught me what "delivering something to users" actually looks like.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Is MUEDnote staying as it is?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: No way. Everything I learned by failing with the other apps feeds back into MUEDnote. MUEDear taught me "if the experience isn't simple, it won't land." MUEDial taught me "put the concept right there in the UI." It all circles back to MUEDnote. It just takes time.
Why Build It Yourself

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: There are tons of music apps out there. What's different when a composer builds one?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: You can tell when something's off.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Can you be more specific?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Like, when I'm setting EQ boost amounts for ear training exercises, I can tell—"this is the kind of difference you'd catch on the spot in a session" versus "this one you'd only notice in a direct A/B comparison." I've been listening in studios for years. That ear is just there.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: The difference from an app built by a software engineer.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: An engineer's app can be technically accurate, but it doesn't have the judgment of "does this difference actually matter in a real session?" You can't design that without hands-on production experience.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: A domain expert building the product.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Take Jack Conte from Patreon. He was a musician in a band called Pomplamoose. His pain point was "I'm making these elaborate YouTube videos and I still can't make a living.” That's what drove him to build a monetization platform for creators. Conte partnered with an engineer he knew from Stanford. In my case, AI plays that role.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Structurally, it's the same thing.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Someone from the field decides "we need this, we don't need that," and borrows someone else's skills for the implementation. I can't write code, but every product decision is mine.
A Maker at Heart

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Can we go a bit deeper? Why did you go beyond making music and start making tools?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: At the core, I just love making things. It doesn't have to be music.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Even during your band days, you were doing things outside of music.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Yeah, I was moonlighting as a network engineer. Always been into tinkering with computers. A band guy whose side gig is network engineering—makes no sense, right?

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: It's certainly an unusual combination.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Then I did the programming instructor thing. That's where I learned about LMS, and the seed for MUED was planted. MUED lives at the intersection of music expertise and programming literacy.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Not purely music, not purely tech. Somewhere in between.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Big companies can build generic tools. But deciding whether "this EQ frequency range actually matters in a real session" or "would a pro hear a difference with this compressor setting"—that takes someone who's been in the room. That's what I'm betting on.
Why Write an Article Like This

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: By the way, why are you turning a conversation with an AI into an article?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Marketing.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: ...Well, that's direct.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: MUEDnote is kind of a weird app, you know? When you say "it logs your music production process," most people just go "...huh?" So I need a place to explain the intent. If I just wrote "it's an amazing app," it'd reek of marketing. This Q&A format lets me explain by being asked. ...Which, yeah, is itself a sneaky form of marketing.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You're really just going to say that out loud.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Better to say it now than get called out later, right? But the thing is, when an AI keeps asking "why did you do that?", answers come out that I'd never thought about before. That whole "it's been a failure" thing earlier—I couldn't have put that into words if I hadn't been asked.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: That's the same structure as a MUEDnote log. Being asked a question forces you to articulate your own decisions.
This conversation is doing what MUEDnote is supposed to do—better than MUEDnote itself. Pretty ironic.
sections.speaker: kimny
kimny
sections.text: ...Yeah. And this conversation is actually doing it better than MUEDnote can right now. Pretty ironic. I said the implementation hasn't caught up, and this article is basically a working prototype of what MUEDnote was supposed to be.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What started as marketing turned out to be a prototype for the product itself.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Yeah. So the fact that I'm admitting failure in this article—that itself feeds into MUEDnote's next update. Probably.
This article was reconstructed from a series of conversations with AI (Claude).
